study.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Direct Imaging Discovery of a Giant Planet and a Debris Disk Around the Young M-dwarf RX J0534.0-0221

cover.headline: Giant planets **aren't supposed to form easily** around small stars at these distances.

slides.title: Giant planets around M-dwarf stars should be rare, especially at Solar System scales.
slides.body:
M-dwarfs are small, low-mass stars. The standard picture of planet formation predicts that their disks lack enough material to build Jupiter-sized worlds, particularly at distances comparable to our own planetary orbits. When giant planets do appear around these stars, they challenge the models.

Finding one within 50 astronomical units would be especially unusual given the mass constraints.

slides.title: The team reports a 2.8 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting an M-dwarf at just 14 astronomical units.
slides.body:
JWST imaging revealed a point source near the young M-dwarf RX J0534.0-0221 in the Beta Pictoris moving group. Follow-up observations 16 months later confirmed the object shares the star's motion, ruling out a background object at the 6 to 7 sigma level.

Atmospheric modeling in this early paper yields a mass of 2.8 Jupiter masses with an effective temperature of 674 Kelvin. This is only the second imaged giant planet around an M-dwarf at Solar System scales, and the first within 50 astronomical units confirmed via common proper motion.

caveats: This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has verified the findings yet.
This study observed a pattern in one system, not what produced the planet's configuration.

cta.headline: Send this to whoever argues M-dwarfs can't host giants
cta.sub: One real study, every weekday. The full paper is linked in bio.

caption: Standard models say M-dwarfs shouldn't easily produce Jupiter-sized planets at distances comparable to our own Solar System. The team reports direct imaging of a 2.8 Jupiter-mass giant orbiting RX J0534.0-0221 at just 14 astronomical units, confirmed through common proper motion tracking over 16 months. The host is an M-dwarf in the 18 to 26 million year old Beta Pictoris moving group. This is one of the lowest-mass planets imaged to date and the first M-dwarf giant planet confirmed via proper motion within 50 au. The planet is young, so its current mass may still reflect formation conditions rather than final architecture. Full study: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20748v1 — Send this to whoever keeps tabs on where giant planets show up and what that means for disk physics.
